Recent work separates complementarity, substitution, and compatibility. [ECCR (2024)](https://genai-personalization.github.io/assets/papers/GenAIRecP2024/Li.pdf) distinguishes items that work together from merely related products; category-level complementarity can still produce incompatible pairs. [Function-Based Labels (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167865525003976) addresses ambiguity through functional relationship labels. These distinctions support diagnostics, but ECCR’s pretrained LLM approach is outside the task’s constraints.

A practical adaptation—not a validated result from these papers—is an evidence ledger using deterministic extraction and corpus-fitted TF–IDF: retain exact title/description spans, item IDs, matched model numbers, explicit compatibility phrases, and contradictions. Label pairs supported, contradicted, or unknown; report metadata availability and the fraction of recommendations with sufficient evidence. Flag repeated titles, editions, or overlapping collections as potential redundancy, not unwanted purchases. For media, measure history overlap with explicitly named artists, franchises, formats, and languages; leave absent attributes unknown. Timestamps establish sequence and recency, not confirmed purchase intent; text supports a compatibility claim, not physical verification or user need.

For uncertainty, report validation risk–coverage curves as diagnostic claims are progressively withheld, stratified by dataset and metadata availability. [Online Selective Conformal Prediction: Errors and Solutions (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16809) shows that selection can break exchangeability and invalidate coverage claims. Consequently, confidence thresholds require separate calibration data and assumption checks; without labeled compatibility or intent outcomes, report evidence coverage and abstention rates rather than claiming calibrated correctness. Keep these diagnostics distinct from the benchmark’s macro validation HR@10.
